q: Who is the author of the lesson "A Letter to God"?
o: Liam O'Flaherty
G.L. Fuentes
Frederick Forsyth
Lucio Rodrigues
e: G.L. Fuentes wrote "A Letter to God". Liam O'Flaherty wrote "His First Flight", Frederick Forsyth wrote "The Black Aeroplane", and Lucio Rodrigues wrote "A Baker from Goa".

q: Where was Lencho's house situated?
o: On the crest of a low hill
At the bottom of the valley
In a town near the river
Inside a forest between hills
e: Lencho's house was the only one in the entire valley and sat on the crest of a low hill, not at the bottom, in town, or in a forest.

q: According to Lencho, what was the only thing the earth needed?
o: Bright sunshine
Irrigation from the river
Strong winds and hailstones
A downpour or at least a shower
e: Lencho felt the field of ripe corn only needed a downpour or at least a shower for a good harvest, not sunshine, hailstones, or river water.

q: Which crop had Lencho grown in his fields?
o: Wheat
Paddy (rice)
Corn
Sugarcane
e: Lencho grew fields of ripe corn dotted with flowers. Wheat, paddy, and sugarcane are not mentioned in the story.

q: In which direction did Lencho look at the sky while waiting for rain?
o: North-west
North-east
South-east
South-west
e: All morning Lencho looked towards the sky in the north-east, from where huge mountains of clouds approached, not any other direction.

q: What did Lencho compare the big and little raindrops to?
o: Ten-cent and five-cent new coins
Pearls and diamonds
Silver ornaments
Grains of salt
e: Lencho called big drops ten-cent pieces and little ones fives (new coins). Hailstones were called frozen pearls/silver coins, and the white field looked covered with salt.

q: Which calamity completely destroyed Lencho's crops?
o: Drought
A plague of locusts
Flood
A hailstorm
e: A severe hailstorm rained for an hour and completely destroyed the corn. A plague of locusts was only mentioned by Lencho in comparison ("would have left more than this").

q: For how long did the hail rain on the valley?
o: For fifteen minutes
For half an hour
For an hour
All through the night
e: According to the text, the hail rained on the house, garden, hillside, cornfield, and whole valley for an hour.

q: What did the boys run out into the rain to collect?
o: Ripe fruits
Frozen pearls (hailstones)
Flower petals
Clothes and utensils
e: Exposing themselves to the rain, the boys ran out to collect the "frozen pearls" (hailstones), not fruits, flowers, or utensils.

q: What was the only hope left in Lencho's heart after the destruction?
o: Help from God
Loan from the postmaster
Compensation from government
Aid from relatives
e: All through the night, Lencho thought only of his one hope: the help of God, not from government, relatives, or the postmaster.

q: How much money did Lencho ask God for in his letter?
o: 70 pesos
1000 pesos
50 pesos
100 pesos
e: Lencho asked God for a hundred pesos to sow his field again and live until the next crop. Seventy pesos was the amount he actually received.

q: On which day did Lencho begin to write the letter to God at daybreak?
o: Monday
Friday
Sunday
Saturday
e: The story states that "the following Sunday, at daybreak", Lencho began writing the letter to carry to town himself.

q: What did Lencho write on the envelope as the address?
o: To the Postmaster
To God
To Heaven
To the Mayor
e: Lencho wrote "To God" on the envelope, put the letter inside, placed a stamp, and dropped it into the mailbox.

q: How much money did Lencho actually receive in the envelope?
o: 70 pesos
30 pesos
100 pesos
50 pesos
e: The postmaster could collect only a little more than half—seventy pesos—to send to Lencho; thirty pesos remained short of the hundred.

q: Which single word was written as a signature in the letter sent by the postmaster?
o: Postmaster
Friend
Blessings
God
e: To preserve Lencho's faith, the postmaster signed the reply letter with only a single word: "God".

q: What did Lencho call the post office employees in his second letter?
o: Kind helpers
Honest officers
A bunch of crooks
Careless workers
e: Finding 30 pesos missing, Lencho assumed God could not make a mistake and called the post office employees "a bunch of crooks" (dishonest people).

q: How is the postmaster described in the story?
o: A thin and angry man
A fat, amiable fellow
A strict and selfish man
A lazy and gloomy man
e: The text describes the postmaster as "a fat, amiable fellow" (friendly and pleasant), not angry, selfish, or lazy.

q: The currency "peso" mentioned in the story is used in several countries of which region?
o: Latin America (e.g., Mexico)
Eastern Europe
Central Asia
Scandinavia
e: According to the NCERT glossary, the peso is the currency of several Latin American countries (G.L. Fuentes was Mexican), not Europe, Central Asia, or Scandinavia.

q: Who composed the poem "Dust of Snow"?
o: Robin Klein
Leslie Norris
John Berryman
Robert Frost
e: Robert Frost composed both "Dust of Snow" and "Fire and Ice". Leslie Norris wrote "A Tiger in the Zoo", John Berryman wrote "The Ball Poem", and Robin Klein wrote "Amanda!".

q: Which bird shook down the dust of snow on the poet in "Dust of Snow"?
o: A sparrow
A pigeon
A crow
A cuckoo
e: The opening lines state: "The way a crow / Shook down on me / The dust of snow", so it was a crow, not a sparrow, pigeon, or cuckoo.

q: Under which tree was the poet standing in the poem "Dust of Snow"?
o: An oak tree
A hemlock tree
A pine tree
A maple tree
e: The poet was under a hemlock tree—a poisonous plant/tree with small white flowers—not an oak, pine, or maple tree.

q: What effect did the falling dust of snow have on the poet?
o: It changed his mood and saved some part of his day
He fell ill from cold
He got angry at the crow
He fell into a deep sleep
e: The dust of snow gave the poet's heart a "change of mood" and saved some part of a day he had regretted, rather than causing illness or anger.

q: What does the word "rued" mean in the poem "Dust of Snow"?
o: Full of joy
Icy and freezing
Completely forgotten
Held in regret
e: In "Of a day I had rued", "rued" means held in regret—the poet regretted wasting his earlier hours until his mood shifted.

q: Which two negative symbols did Robert Frost use as carriers of positivity in "Dust of Snow"?
o: Snow and sky
Leaves and flowers
Crow and hemlock tree
Rain and wind
e: Both the crow and the poisonous hemlock tree are traditionally associated with gloom and ill-omen, yet Frost uses them to bring a positive change of mood.

q: Who wrote the poem "Fire and Ice"?
o: Walt Whitman
Robert Frost
Carl Sandburg
W.B. Yeats
e: "Fire and Ice" is written by Robert Frost. Whitman wrote "Animals", Sandburg wrote "Fog", and Yeats wrote "For Anne Gregory".

q: In the poem "Fire and Ice", what does "Fire" stand for?
o: Uncontrolled desire, greed, and passion
Hatred and rigidity
Love for nature
Patience and peace
e: Frost links fire with desire ("From what I've tasted of desire / I hold with those who favour fire"), whereas ice stands for hatred.

q: In the poem "Fire and Ice", what does "Ice" symbolize?
o: Burning desire
Hope and renewal
Fury and passion
Hatred, coldness, and indifference
e: The poet says "I think I know enough of hate / To say that for destruction ice / Is also great", so ice symbolizes hatred and cold indifference.

q: According to "Fire and Ice", if the world had to perish twice, what would suffice for its destruction?
o: Desire alone
A great flood
Ice (hatred)
Volcanic eruption
e: Frost writes that if the world had to perish twice, ice (representing hatred) is also great and "would suffice".

q: What is the meaning of the word "suffice" in the poem "Fire and Ice"?
o: To suffer pain
To be sufficient
To prevent
To melt away
e: "Suffice" means to be sufficient or enough. Do not confuse it with "suffer" (to undergo pain).

q: What is the rhyme scheme of the poem "Dust of Snow"?
o: abab cdcd
aabb ccdd
abba cddc
aaab cccb
e: In stanza 1, crow/snow (a) and me/tree (b) give abab; in stanza 2, heart/part (c) and mood/rued (d) give cdcd. Hence abab cdcd.

q: What was Lencho's wife doing when Lencho predicted rain?
o: Preparing supper
Working in the fields
Going to the market
Washing clothes
e: The text mentions "The woman who was preparing supper, replied, 'Yes, God willing.'" The older boys were in the field and smaller ones played near the house.

q: Why did Lencho tell his sons that "a plague of locusts would have left more than this"?
o: Because his sons refused to work
Because locusts had attacked the fields
Because there was too little rain
Because the hailstorm left not a single leaf or grain of corn
e: The hail had left nothing—no leaves on trees, no flowers, no corn—whereas even a locust swarm usually leaves behind some remains.

q: What does the expression "Lencho was an ox of a man" mean in the story?
o: Lencho was very lazy
Lencho was illiterate
Lencho was an extremely hardworking man
Lencho was short-tempered
e: The phrase explains that Lencho worked tirelessly like an animal in the fields (very hardworking), "but still he knew how to write" (so he was not illiterate).

q: Who first saw Lencho's letter at the post office, and how did he react?
o: The postmaster; he got angry
A postman; he went to his boss laughing heartily
A clerk; he tore the letter
Lencho's neighbour; he started crying
e: A postman (who also helped at the post office) went to his boss laughing heartily and showed him the letter to God because he had never known that address.

q: How did the postmaster manage to arrange money for Lencho?
o: Gave part of his salary and collected donations from employees and friends
Took money from government funds
Took a bank loan
Mortgaged Lencho's land
e: The postmaster asked his employees for money, contributed part of his own salary, and obliged several friends to give something for "an act of charity".

q: How did Lencho affix the stamp to his second letter?
o: With a bottle of glue
By asking the postman to paste it
Using adhesive tape
By licking it and affixing it with a blow of his fist
e: Lencho bought a stamp at the window, licked it, and affixed it to the envelope with a blow of his fist, showing both his anger and simplicity.

q: Why did Lencho show not the slightest surprise on seeing the money inside the envelope?
o: He knew about the postmaster's generosity
He had informed the bank earlier
Such was his unshakeable confidence and faith in God
He never expected any reply
e: Lencho's confidence in God was so absolute that receiving money from God did not surprise him at all; only finding it short of 100 pesos angered him.

q: Why did Lencho ask God not to send the remaining money through the mail?
o: Because postal service was very slow
Because he believed the post office employees had stolen 30 pesos
Because his house was too far from town
Because he no longer needed money
e: Believing God could never err or deny him, Lencho concluded that the post office staff ("a bunch of crooks") had pocketed the missing 30 pesos.

q: What was the postmaster experiencing from his office as the postman handed the letter to Lencho?
o: The contentment of a man who has performed a good deed
Fear of being mocked
Anger and irritation
Sadness and regret
e: The postmaster looked on from his office, experiencing the contentment of a man who has performed a good deed.

q: What did the flowers dotting Lencho's field of ripe corn promise?
o: An approaching hailstorm
A plague of locusts
A severe drought
A good harvest
e: The opening paragraph explicitly says: "the field of ripe corn dotted with the flowers that always promised a good harvest."

q: Why did Lencho step out into the rain when the raindrops began to fall?
o: To open irrigation channels
To call the younger boys inside
To have the pleasure of feeling the rain on his body
To repair the roof
e: The text states: "The man went out for no other reason than to have the pleasure of feeling the rain on his body."

q: What was the destroyed cornfield compared to after the hailstorm stopped?
o: A sheet of white cotton
Covered with salt
A river of milk
Sand dunes
e: The author writes: "The field was white, as if covered with salt," highlighting both the white expanse of hail and its barren, destructive impact.

q: Why did Lencho wrinkle his brow while writing the second letter at the public writing-table?
o: Because of the effort he had to make to express his ideas
The lighting was very dim
The ink had run out
The postmaster was staring at him
e: The text explains his wrinkled brow was "caused by the effort he had to make to express his ideas" on the public writing-table.

q: Which detail in "A Letter to God" shows Lencho's belief in God's omniscience?
o: God would bring money in person
God reads letters only on Sundays
God lives on the crest of the hill
God's eyes see everything, even what is deep in one's conscience
e: Lencho believed in "the help of God, whose eyes, as he had been instructed, see everything, even what is deep in one's conscience."

q: Why did the postmaster turn serious almost immediately after laughing at Lencho's letter?
o: He was scolded by his boss
The letter contained a threat
He was deeply moved by the writer's immense faith in God
There was too much workload in the office
e: Tapping the letter on his desk, he exclaimed, "What faith! I wish I had the faith of the man who wrote this letter. Starting up a correspondence with God!"

q: What was the poet's state of mind before the dust of snow fell on him?
o: Extremely excited and cheerful
Depressed, sorrowful, and regretful
Celebrating a victory
Furious and vengeful
e: The phrase "a day I had rued" reveals the poet was depressed and full of regret before nature unexpectedly lifted his spirits.

q: What is the central message of Robert Frost's poem "Dust of Snow"?
o: Even small, ordinary moments in nature can bring major positive change to our mood
One should avoid standing under trees in winter
Crows and poisonous trees always bring bad luck
Humans should sleep away gloomy days
e: The poem conveys that simple, tiny occurrences in nature can heal sorrow, shift our perspective, and redeem a wasted day.

q: How many lines and stanzas does the poem "Dust of Snow" have?
o: 16 lines in 4 stanzas
12 lines in 3 stanzas
9 lines in 1 stanza
8 lines divided into 2 stanzas
e: "Dust of Snow" consists of 8 short lines arranged in two 4-line stanzas (whereas "Fire and Ice" has 9 lines).

q: What does "dust of snow" refer to in the poem?
o: Road dust mixed with ice
Large hard hailstones
Fine powdery particles of snow resting on the tree
Thick white fog
e: "Dust of snow" refers to the fine, powdery flakes/particles of snow lying on the branches of the hemlock tree that fall gently on the poet.

q: In "Fire and Ice", which view about the end of the world does the poet favour first?
o: Those who favour ice
Those who favour fire (desire)
Those who believe the world will never end
Those who predict destruction by flood
e: Frost states, "From what I've tasted of desire / I hold with those who favour fire," showing he initially sides with fire.

q: Which words rhyme with "twice" in the poem "Fire and Ice"?
o: ice and suffice
fire and desire
hate and great
say and world
e: In "Fire and Ice", "twice" rhymes with "ice" and "suffice". "Hate" rhymes with "great", and "fire" rhymes with "desire".

q: What is the central idea of the poem "Fire and Ice"?
o: Science alone will save the planet
The Earth will end only from solar heat
Humans should only fear cold winters
Both uncontrolled desire (fire) and cold hatred (ice) can destroy humanity
e: Frost symbolically warns that humanity's extreme passions—unbridled desire (fire) and cold hatred/indifference (ice)—are equally capable of causing destruction.

q: Whose opinions about the end of the world are presented in the opening two lines of "Fire and Ice"?
o: Only scientists
Only ancient poets
People in general ("Some say...")
Lencho and his sons
e: The poem opens with "Some say the world will end in fire / Some say in ice," reflecting two contrasting popular beliefs among people.

q: In "Dust of Snow", what happened strictly because of the crow's movement on the hemlock tree?
o: The tree got uprooted
Fine dust of snow fell down on the poet
The crow sat on the poet's shoulder
White flowers scattered on the road
e: The crow's movement dislodged fine particles of snow from the hemlock tree onto the poet, unexpectedly shifting his gloomy mood.

q: What did Lencho conclude when he counted only 70 pesos in the envelope?
o: God could neither make a mistake nor deny him; the postal staff took the rest
The postmaster kindly donated his own money
God must have run short of money
30 pesos were lost in transit due to rain
e: Lencho instantly thought God could not have made a mistake or denied his request, convincing him that the postal employees stole the missing 30 pesos.

q: Which foreign currency word is used in "A Letter to God" to reflect its Latin American setting?
o: Franc
Ruble
Pound
Peso
e: The story uses the "peso", reflecting its Latin American setting. Francs appear in "The Necklace" and rubles in "The Proposal".

q: Why did the postmaster decide to answer Lencho's letter?
o: He wanted to continue the joke
It was a postal rule to reply to every letter
In order not to shake the writer's faith in God
He wanted to buy Lencho's farm
e: The text explicitly says: "So, in order not to shake the writer's faith in God, the postmaster came up with an idea: answer the letter."

q: What does the word "perish" mean in the line "But if it had to perish twice"?
o: To grow
To die or be destroyed
To shine brightly
To freeze solid
e: "Perish" means to die, decay, or come to an end—referring here to the destruction of the world a second time.

q: According to "Dust of Snow", how much of the poet's day was saved?
o: Some part of a day
The entire day and night
Only one minute
The whole week
e: The poet says it "saved some part / Of a day I had rued"—meaning the remainder of the day was rescued from gloom and regret.

q: When did Lencho go to the post office to check for God's reply?
o: The same evening
The next Wednesday evening
After a full month
The following Sunday, a bit earlier than usual
e: The story states: "The following Sunday Lencho came a bit earlier than usual to ask if there was a letter for him."

q: Read the line: "It was during the meal that, just as Lencho had predicted, big drops of rain began to fall." What quality of Lencho does this reflect?
o: His magical power to control weather
His formal training as a meteorologist
His impatience and nervousness
His intimate knowledge of his fields and sky patterns as an experienced farmer
e: Lencho "knew his fields intimately"; observing the sky towards the north-east allowed him to accurately predict rain from lived farming experience.

q: Extract: "The air was fresh and sweet. The man went out for no other reason than to have the pleasure of feeling the rain on his body." What mood is Lencho in here?
o: Fear and suspicion
Anger and irritation
Pure joy, relief, and optimism
Indifference
e: The sensory words "fresh and sweet" and "pleasure" show Lencho's pure joy, relief, and optimism about a thriving harvest.

q: Lencho calling raindrops "new coins" ("The big drops are ten cent pieces and the little ones are fives") is an example of which literary device?
o: Simile
Metaphor
Alliteration
Hyperbole
e: Saying raindrops "are new coins" directly equates two things without "like" or "as", making it a Metaphor (unlike "as if covered with salt", which is a Simile).

q: In "These truly did resemble new silver coins", what are "these", and how does this contrast with Lencho's earlier "new coins"?
o: Raindrops symbolized prosperity, whereas hailstones only looked like silver coins while actually destroying his crop
Both phrases refer literally to actual coins
The hailstones proved valuable like real silver
It describes stamps at the post office
e: Raindrops were life-giving "coins" of prosperity, whereas hailstones merely resembled silver coins visually while bringing ruin.

q: In "The postmaster—a fat, amiable fellow", which word is closest in meaning to "amiable"?
o: Harsh and cruel
Dull and careless
Arrogant and stubborn
Friendly and pleasant
e: "Amiable" means friendly, kind-hearted, and pleasant, matching the postmaster's subsequent charitable behaviour.

q: What does the word "conscience" mean in "even what is deep in one's conscience"?
o: Physical height and strength
A physical illness
An inner moral sense of right and wrong
Pure memory power
e: "Conscience" refers to a person's inner moral sense of right and wrong.

q: In "several friends of his were obliged to give something 'for an act of charity'", what does "obliged" imply here?
o: Fearful of legal punishment
Bound by moral goodwill or politely persuaded to contribute
Under heavy bank debt
Refused to donate anything
e: Here "obliged" means politely persuaded or morally bound out of goodwill to contribute to an act of charity.

q: Extract: "God: Of the money that I asked for, only seventy pesos reached me, send me the rest, since I need it very much." What is Lencho's tone here?
o: Direct, demanding, and indignant
Humble gratitude and satisfaction
Playful and humorous
Doubtful and fearful
e: Lencho offers no thanks for the 70 pesos; instead, he writes directly and indignantly demanding the rest, assuming the postal staff cheated him.

q: Lencho's complete trust in God contrasted with instant distrust of fellow humans highlights which trait in him?
o: His shrewd business cunning
His deep gratitude toward strangers
His scientific rationalism
His naive simplicity and lack of worldly awareness
e: Lencho's faith is pure yet naive—he fails to consider that human kindness could be God's instrument of help.

q: What emotion is emphasized by Lencho's lines "The hail has left nothing" and "A plague of locusts would have left more than this"?
o: Mild disappointment
Eagerness to sell the farm
Utter despair and total devastation
Excitement to visit town
e: Standing in the ruined field, Lencho expresses utter despair and total devastation, feeling even locusts are less cruel than that hailstorm.

q: When the postmaster saw that answering the letter needed "something more than goodwill, ink and paper", what was that "something more"?
o: New seeds and fertilizers
Money (one hundred pesos)
Legal documents
An irrigation pump
e: Opening the letter showed that mere sympathy or a written note was not enough—Lencho explicitly needed money (100 pesos) to survive and re-sow.

q: Which quality best describes Lencho writing simply "To God" on the envelope?
o: Childlike, simple, and unquestioning faith
Cunning and deceit
Complete illiteracy
Pride and arrogance
e: Lencho was literate, yet his faith was so simple and unquestioning that he genuinely believed "To God" was a deliverable address.

q: In "A Letter to God", what does the word "solitary" refer to ("in the middle of the valley, there was a single hope... solitary house")?
o: Crowded and busy
Old and crumbling
Built strongly of stone
Existing alone; single and isolated
e: "Solitary" means single or isolated—living in that solitary house in the middle of the valley meant no neighbours could help him, leaving only God.

q: In "Dust of Snow", a single sentence flows continuously across all lines without punctuation pauses at line ends. Which poetic device is this?
o: Alliteration
Personification
Enjambment
Simile
e: When a sentence continues without punctuation across line breaks onto the next line, it is called Enjambment. The entire 8-line poem is one continuous sentence.

q: Which poetic device is clearly seen in the line "Has given my heart" from "Dust of Snow"?
o: Hyperbole
Alliteration (repetition of the initial /h/ sound in "Has" and "heart")
Pun
Oxymoron
e: The repetition of the initial consonant sound /h/ in "Has" and "heart" (and /s/ in "saved some") is Alliteration.

q: Which sound device is prominent in the line "Shook down on me" in "Dust of Snow"?
o: Assonance (prominence of the "o" vowel sound)
Pun
Irony
Refrain
e: The repetition/prominence of the vowel sound "o" in "Shook down on" is an example of Assonance.

q: In "Dust of Snow", how do the crow and the hemlock tree function differently from traditional poetry?
o: Unlike romantic poets using nightingales or oak trees, Frost uses harsh, gloomy symbols to bring joy
Both crow and hemlock are traditionally seen as symbols of romance
They only serve to give a weather report
The poet hated all elements of nature
e: Whereas traditional poems pick pleasant symbols like nightingales or maples, Frost deliberately uses the gloomy crow and poisonous hemlock to show unexpected healing.

q: In the line "Has given my heart / A change of mood", what does "my heart" represent?
o: Only his physical organ
His lost belongings
The poet's entire emotional self and inner state of mind
The crow's nest
e: Here "my heart" stands for the poet's entire emotional being and inner feelings—a classic literary use of part representing whole.

q: Which poetic device is used at the start of "Some say the world will end in fire, / Some say in ice."?
o: Pun
Anaphora (repetition of "Some say") and Antithesis (Fire vs Ice)
Epithet
Hyperbole
e: Repeating "Some say" at the beginning of consecutive lines is Anaphora, while contrasting "fire" and "ice" shows Antithesis.

q: What does the phrasal verb "hold with" mean in "I hold with those who favour fire"?
o: To agree with or support a view
To hold hands tightly
To stop or restrain someone
To fight against
e: "Hold with" is an idiom meaning to agree with or approve of an opinion.

q: In "I hold with those who favour fire", which two sound devices are present?
o: Oxymoron and Epigram
Simile and Pun
Personification and Metaphor
Alliteration ("favour fire") and Assonance (prominent long "o" in "hold", "those")
e: "favour fire" repeats the /f/ consonant sound (Alliteration), while "hold" and "those" highlight the long "o" vowel sound (Assonance).

q: Treating Fire and Ice as active forces capable of destroying the world ("for destruction ice / Is also great") exemplifies which poetic device?
o: Irony only
Alliteration only
Personification and Symbolism
Onomatopoeia
e: Fire and Ice symbolize human emotions (desire and hate) and are personified as mighty forces able to bring destruction.

q: How does the poet contrast his knowledge of "desire" and "hate" in "Fire and Ice"?
o: He is completely unfamiliar with both emotions
He has personally experienced ("tasted") desire and also knows enough about human hatred
He knows hate well but has never felt desire
He considers both emotions positive virtues
e: Frost says he has "tasted" desire (experienced its burning force) and also "knows enough" about hate to recognize its equal destructiveness.

q: What is the rhyme scheme of the 9-line poem "Fire and Ice"?
o: aba abc bcb
abab cdcd e
aabb ccdd e
abcb abcb a
e: End words are fire(a), ice(b), desire(a), fire(a), twice(b), hate(c), ice(b), great(c), suffice(b), yielding abaabcbcb (aba abc bcb).

q: What does Lencho's line "since I need it very much" in his second letter reveal about his situation?
o: He wanted to buy luxuries
He wanted to reward the post office staff
He planned a vacation to the city
He genuinely needed the remaining 30 pesos to re-sow his field and feed his family
e: Lencho genuinely needed the full 100 pesos to survive until the next harvest and re-sow his ruined field, so 70 pesos felt insufficient.

q: In "A Letter to God", how does the postmaster's sudden seriousness after laughing create a turning point in the plot?
o: He files a police complaint against Lencho
He shuts down the post office
What seemed comical turns into an inspiring act of human empathy and charity
He throws Lencho's letter into the trash
e: His shift from laughter to awe turns a funny incident into a deeply humane act of charity aimed at protecting Lencho's faith.

q: What are "locusts" mentioned in "A plague of locusts would have left more than this"?
o: Freshwater fish
Insects that fly in huge swarms and destroy crops
Small pellets of ice
Cold mountain winds
e: Per the NCERT glossary, locusts are insects that fly in big swarms (groups) and destroy crops.

q: Calling ice "great" for destruction ("To say that for destruction ice / Is also great") creates what poetic effect?
o: Understatement and irony emphasizing how quietly devastating cold hatred is
Praise for the scenic beauty of glaciers
Affection for winter sports
Silly exaggeration
e: Using restrained, conversational words like "great" and "suffice" for world destruction creates powerful understatement and irony.

q: Which phrase in "Dust of Snow" directly signals the turning point in the poet's emotional state?
o: "From a hemlock tree"
"I had rued"
"The way a crow"
"A change of mood"
e: "A change of mood" directly marks the emotional shift from gloom and regret to renewed positivity.

q: Before the meal was called, how did the activities of Lencho's older boys differ from the smaller ones?
o: All the boys had gone to the post office
The older boys slept inside while the smaller ones went to town
The older boys were working in the field while the smaller ones played near the house
The smaller boys ploughed the field while older ones cooked

q: At which point does the sharpest situational irony emerge in "A Letter to God"?

e: Situational irony occurs when an outcome starkly reverses expectations: the postal staff sacrificed their own money to preserve Lencho's faith, yet he condemns them as thieves.

q: How are the two conflicts—"humans vs nature" and "humans vs humans"—illustrated in "A Letter to God"?

To leave readers directly confronting the poignant irony between selfless human kindness and naive human distrust, without moralizing

q: Why do you think Robert Frost kept "The way a crow / Shook down on me" deliberately ambiguous about the crow's exact action?

e: Whether the crow alighted, shivered, or took off does not matter; leaving it open underscores how effortless and unpremeditated nature's healing touch can be.

q: Why can "Dust of Snow" be read as an example of optimistic realism rather than naive romanticism?

It invents a magical fairyland
It advises cutting down poisonous trees
e: Frost neither denies regret ("rued") nor relies on pretty clichés; he finds real emotional rescue through stark, unglamorous symbols—a crow and a hemlock.

q: Examine the grammatical link between Stanza 1 and Stanza 2 in "Dust of Snow". How are they connected?

e: The entire poem is one single sentence: Stanza 1 introduces the subject/cause ("The way a crow..."), and Stanza 2 supplies the verb/effect ("Has given... and saved...").

q: How does "Dust of Snow" challenge common human superstitions about crows and winter gloom?

It claims only summer weather brings happiness
It dismantles superstition by showing that supposedly "inauspicious" things like crows and poison trees can trigger renewal and joy
e: By making a crow and a poisonous hemlock rescue the speaker's mood, Frost subverts superstitions and shows beauty/healing can arise from anything.

q: Why is the verb "tasted" particularly effective in "From what I've tasted of desire" in "Fire and Ice"?

e: "Tasted" suggests intimate, first-hand yet limited exposure—even a brief taste of greed or obsession reveals its capacity to consume everything.

q: In "Fire and Ice", what tone does the understated phrase "I think I know enough of hate" create?

A restrained, thoughtful understatement backed by sobering observation of human cruelty

A loud political shout
e: Frost uses quiet understatement ("I think", "also great", "would suffice") to deliver a chilling truth about human hatred without melodrama.

The poem applied solely to the past
Modern technology has eliminated desire and hate
e: Endless greed, aggression, and consumerism represent "fire", while prejudice, intolerance, and apathy toward suffering represent "ice"—both threaten humanity today.

q: Although fire and ice are physical opposites, how are they shown to be identical in outcome in "Fire and Ice"?
o: Both enrich soil fertility
Both have the exact same physical temperature
Both occur only inside volcanoes
Extreme heat and extreme cold both kill life; similarly, blazing passion/greed and icy hatred equally destroy relationships and humanity
e: Paradoxically, polar opposites—extreme heat (desire) and extreme cold (hatred)—converge on the exact same outcome: total destruction.

q: What flaw in reasoning is revealed when Lencho thinks, "God could not have made a mistake, nor could he have denied Lencho what he had requested"?
o: He thought pesos had lost currency value
He miscounted 70 pesos as 80 pesos
He never considered that God might work through ordinary humans whose own financial means were limited
He mailed the letter to the wrong country
e: Lencho's rigid logic assumes God literally mails exact cash directly, leaving him incapable of imagining compassionate humans pooling what little they could afford.

q: What effect does the phrase "It was nothing less than a letter to God" create in the narrative?
o: It implies the letter was trivial and unimportant
It highlights the extraordinary, almost unbelievable audacity and sincerity of Lencho's direct faith in God
It labels Lencho clinically insane
It shows he wrote to many relatives first
e: The emphatic phrasing "nothing less than" underscores how astonishing and unprecedented it was for a farmer to literally write directly to God.

q:
Arrange these events from "A Letter to God" in chronological order:
1. Postmaster collects 70 pesos
2. Lencho compares raindrops to coins
3. Postman laughs and shows the letter
4. Lencho affixes a stamp with a blow of his fist
e: Order: Raindrops as coins (2) → After hail and letter #1, postman laughs showing it (3) → Postmaster gathers 70 pesos (1) → After counting 70 pesos, Lencho writes letter #2 and slams the stamp (4).

q: How does the pairing of "crow" and "hemlock tree" reflect Robert Frost's distinctive poetic style?
o: Celebrating only urban machinery
Relying on Greek mythology
Using ornate Latin vocabulary
Using ordinary, realistic, and unglamorous rural imagery to express profound psychological truth
e: Frost is celebrated for taking stark, everyday rural elements and simple diction to convey deep emotional and philosophical insights.

q: What structural feature do "Dust of Snow" (8 lines) and "Fire and Ice" (9 lines) share, and how does it enhance their impact?
o: Both achieve striking brevity—packing profound psychological and universal themes into tight, memorable rhyming lines
Both are sprawling multi-page epics
Both are unrhymed prose paragraphs
Both list historical dates
e: Their concise length and crisp rhyme schemes concentrate huge philosophical weight into a few memorable lines—like a poetic aphorism.

q: Based on the postmaster's character in "A Letter to God", how would he most likely react internally after reading Lencho's second letter?
o: He would sue Lencho in court for defamation
Despite feeling startled or hurt by the irony, his amiable and compassionate nature would make him smile at Lencho's unshakeable, naive faith
He would march up the hill and take back the 70 pesos
He would fire every employee at the post office
e: Portrayed as an amiable, empathetic man who acted purely for charity and faith, he would recognize the irony with bittersweet amusement rather than vengeance.

q: Why did Lencho carry the letter to town himself and place it in the mail rather than sending one of his sons?
o: Because it was an intensely personal, urgent plea to God upon which his family's survival depended
Because his sons had never visited town
Because he planned a secret meeting with the postmaster
Because he had no pen at home
e: Carrying the letter himself shows the solemn urgency and deep personal devotion of a head of household placing his family's survival directly in God's hands.

q: Putting together "I hold with those who favour fire" and "for destruction ice / Is also great", what is Frost's ultimate verdict?
o: Hatred is morally superior to desire
Fire is dangerous while ice is completely harmless
Humans should cultivate greater desire
Whether driven by hot obsession or cold hatred, either extreme human vice is enough to destroy us, so both must be checked
e: Frost refuses to rank one vice as harmless; both fiery desire and icy hatred carry equal destructive potential unless humanity exercises restraint.

q: In "A Letter to God", who reminds whom of the saying "That's what they say: no one dies of hunger", and what does it reflect?
o: The postman says this as a joke while laughing
The postmaster writes this proverb inside the reply envelope
Lencho reassures himself with this folk saying during the night of despair, showing how deeply his traditional faith sustains hope
Lencho's wife sings this during dinner
e: Despite earlier fearing starvation, Lencho draws quiet strength from this proverb ("no one dies of hunger"), anchoring his decision to seek God's help.

q: Which element in "Dust of Snow" acts as the "unexpected catalyst" that transforms the speaker's mood?
o: Warm bright sunlight breaking through clouds
The fine dust of snow shaken down from the hemlock tree by a crow
A comforting letter from an old friend
A sweet melody sung by a nightingale
e: Rather than wise advice or spring birdsong, an unremarkable crow shaking powdery snow off a poisonous hemlock unexpectedly sparks emotional renewal.

q: What creates dramatic tension in the final scene as Lencho asks for paper and ink at the post office window?
o: Readers know the postal staff themselves donated the 70 pesos, watching helplessly as an angry Lencho drafts a complaint accusing them of theft
The postmaster is calling the police to arrest Lencho
Lencho refuses to pay for paper and ink
A fire breaks out inside the mail room
e: Dramatic irony peaks because the audience knows the postmaster's selfless truth while Lencho ignorantly writes an accusation right under their eyes.
